1.goal: To open on a question she is already being asked constantly, and to say once where the hour ends.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class and whether she wrote the three questions for Nina.
Say what today is: two minutes about herself, now, with no help, and the same two minutes again at the end.
Ask the question on screen and take whatever comes.
exact: What today is: “Two minutes about you, right now, with nothing. Then we do it again at the end of the hour, and we compare.”
1.expected: A number, and probably some irritation about being asked. Both are useful.
1.support: If she says nothing, ask who asks her most often: family, school, or people she has just met.
1.challenge: Ask what she usually answers, and whether it is true.
1.monitoring: Whether the subject is live for her. Her profile says it is, and it will show here.
1.evidence: How she talks about the question itself. It shapes how you run screen 10.
1.transition: Move on as soon as she knows the two minutes are coming twice.

2.goal: To set the situation, the person and the time limit, so the first attempt has a shape.
run: Read Nina's card with her, including the line that says she is made up.
Read the four things on the list and ask the question: what does Nina need first, and what can wait?
Do not discuss how to say any of it. That is later.
2.expected: What she studies first, then what she wants to do. The reason and the question back are the two people usually leave out.
2.support: Ask what she would want to hear first if she were the one who had just arrived.
2.challenge: Ask what Nina will ask about if she only hears the first two.
2.monitoring: Whether she anticipates the reason as something Nina will want.
2.evidence: What she thinks can wait. It usually predicts what she leaves out on screen 3.
2.transition: Move on when the four are on the table and the two minutes are about to start.

3.goal: To collect two minutes of unprepared speech as the baseline of the whole block.
3.interaction: S alone, speaking to you as Nina. You listen and say almost nothing.
run: Start the two minutes and stay quiet. Do not nod her along, do not supply words, do not correct.
If she stops early, wait. The pause is part of what is being measured.
Only if the silence goes past twenty seconds, ask one of Nina's four questions and go quiet again.
Write down how long she spoke and roughly how many sentences came out.
exact: Starting it: “I am Nina. We have got two minutes before the break ends. Tell me about you.”
After a long silence, one question only: “And what do you want to do after school?”
3.expected: Somewhere between four and eight sentences. Her profile says two or three is normal, so this is already a stretch and it is meant to be.
3.support: None. This screen has no support by design, and adding any destroys what it exists to measure.
3.challenge: Say nothing at all for the whole two minutes and see how far she goes.
3.monitoring: Length, number of sentences, whether a reason appears, and what she does when she runs out.
3.evidence: The baseline of the block: how long, how many sentences, and what she left out. Everything on screen 10 is compared against this.
3.transition: Move on when the two minutes are up, whatever happened. Say nothing evaluative yet.

4.goal: To see Nina's four questions and identify which one has no prepared answer.
4.interaction: T–S, reading the four out loud.
run: Read the four questions out loud, one at a time.
Ask which is the hard one and what makes it hard.
Do not answer it yet. Screen 7 is where that happens.
4.expected: The fourth. What makes it hard is that it has no answer, not that it has hard words.
4.support: Ask her to answer the first three quickly out loud, so the fourth stands out by itself.
4.challenge: Ask whether she could answer the fourth one in Portuguese.
4.monitoring: Whether she separates a hard question from hard vocabulary. They are different problems.
4.evidence: What she says makes the fourth question hard.
4.transition: Move on once the fourth has been named.

5.goal: To read one model answer and compare it with what she said seven minutes ago.
run: Let her read it once on her own.
Ask the question on the screen: what does Rafa do that she did not?
Take her answer before you say anything. She usually sees it herself.
5.expected: He gives a reason, he says he is not sure, and he asks a question back. Most people notice the reason first and the doubt second.
5.support: If nothing comes, ask her to find the sentence where he says he does not know.
5.challenge: Ask which of Rafa's sentences she would not be comfortable saying, and why.
5.monitoring: Whether she notices the doubt as a strength rather than as a gap.
5.evidence: What she identifies as missing from her own version. It is worth more than anything you could tell her.
5.transition: Move on when she has named at least one difference.

6.goal: To sort the model into the three kinds of sentence, and see that all three are needed.
run: Let her sort the six lines.
Check them, and then ask two questions: what happens if you take the doubts out, and what happens if you take the reasons out?
Count them at the end: two of each.
6.expected: Two facts, two reasons, two doubts. Without the doubts it sounds rehearsed; without the reasons there is nothing to ask about.
6.support: Ask, on each line: is this something you can check, something that explains, or something you do not know?
6.challenge: Ask which of the three kinds she used on screen 3, and which she did not.
6.monitoring: Whether she can name the kind that was missing from her own first attempt.
6.evidence: Which of the three she was already using before the lesson.
6.transition: Move on once the six are sorted and the two questions have been answered.

7.goal: To have three ways of answering a question she has no answer to.
run: Let her mark the three.
Check them, and say the difference out loud: the three that work all buy a little time and then say something.
Point out that the first phrase in the first answer comes from the last lesson and works here unchanged.
7.expected: The three that keep her in the conversation. I do not know is the one most often accepted, because it is honest.
7.support: Ask, on each one: what can the other person say after this?
7.challenge: Ask her to give a fourth answer of her own that would also work.
7.monitoring: Whether she sees that the difference is not honesty but whether there is anything left to say.
7.evidence: Whether she marked the apology about her English. It says something about how she reads her own level.
7.transition: Move on when the three are settled.

8.goal: To write one sentence of each kind and then say all three without looking.
8.interaction: S writes alone for a minute, then says them to you.
run: Give her one minute and quiet. Writing first is how she produces her best sentences.
Then ask her to turn the paper over and say the three.
If one of them was better on paper than out loud, say so and let her say it again.
exact: Before she starts: “One minute, three lines. Then the paper goes away.”
8.expected: Three sentences, and the doubt one is the hardest to say out loud even when it is written down.
8.support: The three openings are on screen while she writes. They come off when she speaks.
8.challenge: Ask for a second reason, different from the first.
8.monitoring: The gap between what she writes and what she says. Her profile suggests there will be one.
8.evidence: Whether the written version and the spoken version were the same length.
8.transition: Move on when the three have been said without the paper.

9.goal: To answer four unprepared questions in two sentences each.
9.interaction: T–S, quick-fire. You improvise the questions.
run: Ask four questions she has not seen, built from things she said on screen 3.
Each answer has two parts: the answer, and one more thing.
Keep the pace up. Do not stop to fix anything.
exact: Setting it up: “Four questions you have not seen. Two sentences each — the answer, and then one more thing.”
9.expected: Four two-sentence answers. The second sentence is the whole exercise; the first one always comes.
9.support: If only one sentence comes, wait, and then say “and?” once.
9.challenge: Ask something she cannot possibly have thought about before.
9.monitoring: Whether the second sentence arrives without the prompt.
9.evidence: How many of the four carried two sentences unprompted.
9.transition: Move on when four questions have been answered.

10.goal: To run the whole conversation, with nothing on the screen.
run: Ask her to put away everything she has written before you start.
Run the whole thing: her two minutes, your four questions, and space for one of hers.
Do not correct anything and do not help. If she stalls, ask a question and let her recover.
Write down the length and the number of sentences, the same way you did on screen 3.
exact: Starting it: “Same break, same two minutes. Everything away.”
The unprepared question, asked in the middle and not at the end: “And what if it does not work out?”
10.expected: Longer than screen 3, with a reason, a doubt and a question back. That is the shape the hour built.
10.support: None on screen. If she stalls twice, ask one of Nina's questions and go quiet again.
10.challenge: Answer one of her questions with something unexpected and see whether she follows it up.
10.monitoring: Length and sentence count, against screen 3. Note the reason, the doubt and the question back separately.
10.evidence: The second measurement of the block, and half of the comparison this lesson exists to produce.
10.transition: Move on when the conversation reaches its natural end.

11.goal: To take one point and turn one sentence into a better version of itself.
run: Write one thing that worked and one thing to build on. One of each.
Choose one sentence she actually said and write it in the first box, exactly as it came out.
Let her write the improved version herself in the second box. Do not write it for her.
Tell her she will use that sentence in the next round.
exact: Handing over the rewrite: “That is what you said. Write it the way you would say it now — you, not me.”
11.expected: One sentence, improved by her. Usually the improvement is a reason added, not a grammar fix.
11.support: If she cannot see what to change, ask what Nina would have asked next about that sentence.
11.challenge: Ask her to improve it twice: once shorter, once with more in it.
11.monitoring: Whether her own idea of better is about correctness or about saying more. The second is the one this block wants.
11.evidence: Her upgraded sentence, in her words. It goes into the record.
11.transition: Move on to the second round with the upgraded sentence in hand.

12.goal: To run the conversation once more with the roles reversed, so that she has to get in.
12.interaction: T–S. You talk first and ask nothing for a minute.
run: Start by telling her about Nina's life, and ask her nothing at all for the first minute.
Let her find the way in. Do not open a space for her.
When she has said her three parts and used the upgraded sentence, let her end the conversation.
Then open the comparison button and read it with her.
exact: If she has not got in after ninety seconds: “Do you want to ask me something?”
12.expected: She interrupts or asks something inside the first minute. This is the hardest thing in the lesson and the clearest measure of initiative.
12.support: None, until ninety seconds have passed.
12.challenge: Talk continuously and leave only very small gaps.
12.monitoring: How long it takes her to get in, and whether she used her upgraded sentence.
12.evidence: Whether she entered the conversation without being invited. Note the time.
12.transition: Move on to the close once the comparison has been read.

13.goal: To close the lesson and the block, and to say what the four lessons produced.
13.interaction: T–S, ticking the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Then say the block out loud: the two versions of the two minutes, and the difference between them.
Ask the last question on the screen: which of the four lessons changed most about the way she talks?
exact: Closing the block: “The first two minutes today had nothing. The last ones had an hour. That difference is what these four lessons were.”
13.expected: Her own reading of the four lessons. It goes into the record next to yours.
13.support: If she cannot choose a lesson, offer the two you saw most of in today's speech.
13.challenge: Ask what she wants more of in the next four.
13.monitoring: Whether what she names matches what you observed across the block.
13.evidence: Her answer to the last question. It is the first thing the plan for the next four lessons reads.
13.transition: End here. The block is closed, and the next four are planned from what you wrote down today.
